turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Saturday, the tenth of October. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
A human rights judge wins the Peace Prize on Friday morning. By Friday evening Washington has sanctioned the court she sat on.
[curious] A catastrophe bond is about to watch a category four hurricane come ashore and pay out absolutely nothing.
And the relief scheme for the haze opens above a reading this island has not reached.
[thoughtful] That last one is the whole issue, isn't it. Every desk this week is about a line somebody drew.

The spine is the threshold. Where the number sits, and who put it there. The Norwegian Nobel Committee gave the twenty twenty-six Peace Prize to Navanethem Pillay. Navi Pillay. She's eighty-five. One sentence. For her efforts to promote peace and international law. Twelve million kronor, from two hundred and eighty-seven nominations.
And the committee was not coy about why.
It said international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity.
[thoughtful] Which is a sentence you only write when you think the thing is in danger.
Hours later the Treasury's sanctions office published a new entry. Not a person. An institution, at an address.
Wait — they listed the building?
International Criminal Court, Oude Waalsdorperweg, The Hague. Established the first of July, two thousand and two.
[gasps] They put the founding date on the listing.
The Secretary of State left nothing between the lines. Either the court will end its threats, or we will end the court.
Okay. But you told me this morning the headline isn't the headline.
Read the small print. The same day they issued four general licences — transactions, telecoms and software, pensions, detainees. And a hundred and eighty days before the listing bites.
[skeptical] A hundred and eighty days is not a demolition. That's a negotiating position.

That's the read. William Schabas of Middlesex University London won't call it fatal. They have been developing a plan B on how to get around this. His detail is the useful part — the court has spent over a year migrating off American software, and it has ended its relationship with its insurer.
[curious] So it saw this coming.
Its deputy prosecutor said in September, before the listing, that they'd done a lot of work to ensure the court is buffered.
What would actually settle it?
Whether an American-exposed bank, insurer or cloud provider drops the court inside the window anyway. That's the number to watch, and nobody has it yet.
Eight foreign ministers went in together, didn't they.
Britain, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Canada and Japan. Jointly — regret and strongly disagree.
And the court's own line?
The court cannot stand alone.
[pause] One caution, because the ordering invites it.
Nothing we could read says the designation answered the prize. Hours after is not because of. We're not printing that link.
Good. Now the one that's been sitting in my chest all morning.
Madrid. She was eighty-seven and everyone called her Maricarmen.
[sighs] Tell it properly.

An international investment fund bought her rent-controlled building and put the rent up more than two hundred per cent, to about one thousand seven hundred and fifty euros a month. Seven years. On the twenty-third of September she was carried out of the flat on a stretcher. She died in hospital on Wednesday the seventh — hours before she was due to sign the agreement that would have put her back.
[exhales] Hours.
From her hospital bed she'd asked for one thing. I want what happened to me to help ensure that it doesn't happen to other people.
And the crowd outside parliament? A protester told an American broadcast programme: she's a woman who died of heartbreak. They killed her through heartbreak.
Spain's housing deficit is about seven hundred and fifty thousand homes, and the Bank of Spain expects it to pass one million by twenty twenty-eight.
Average rent against a young person's salary?
Ninety-eight point seven per cent of it.
[deadpan] So the rent is the salary.
Parliament dissolved on Monday after lawmakers rejected an emergency housing bill with an eviction moratorium. Election on the twenty-ninth of November.
And the threshold, in her case, is a signature.
The tenancy existed. The signature did not.
All right. The money block. And you have a model that broke.

For three issues this desk has printed the share of gold's move explained by real yields. Ninety-one per cent, then a hundred and six, then about ninety-eight. This week, on the only window where both endpoints are published, the ten-year real yield fell five basis points. On the quarter's own regression that should have lifted gold about half a per cent. Gold fell.
[scoffs] So it didn't just weaken. It inverted.
The share isn't small. It's sign-inverted. And the whole of gold's weekly gain landed on Friday — the one day the real yield has not been published.
[amused] Of course it did.
The honest version is that we don't know, and the model that worked for three weeks did not work this week.
I want to flag what you did there, because it's rare. You printed your own thing failing.

We also corrected ourselves. Yesterday this desk put the ten-year term premium at a post-June-two-thousand-and-fourteen high. Both halves checked out. But the New York Fed's own daily workbook now has Thursday's reading six and a half basis points below that peak — the largest one-day fall of the episode.
And a major wire ran the regime story on Friday citing the old number.
A figure its own source had already revised away from. That's the week in one sentence.
[wry] Everyone's reading yesterday's spreadsheet.

Singapore, then. The haze turned on Friday night and then it stopped turning. The Central region's twenty-four-hour index reached one hundred and ninety-two at five on Friday afternoon and sat there for four consecutive hours. The season's high. One hundred and seventy-seven at five. Every region still above a hundred. Flattened, not cleared.
And this is where the threshold bites.

The task force convened on Friday — the environment agency and twenty-eight others. The relief is real and specific. Free masks from vending machines at transport hubs. Air-conditioned shelters at community clubs. Preschools to stop strenuous indoor activity.
All of it beginning at? [pause] So this weekend there's a very large crowd standing outdoors at Marina Bay in Unhealthy air, no free masks and no shelters open.
Because the island has not reached the number at which they open. The agency's own forecast is Unhealthy to Low Very Unhealthy — which is to say, possibly just across it.
And then the bit I genuinely did not believe.
The agency publishes four bands for the hourly reading. Band one is fifty-five and below. Band two is fifty-six to one hundred and fifty.
And bands three and four?
No published range. At all.
[gasps] The two bands that mean it's actually bad are the two with no numbers.
The same page says that in significant haze about one in ten hourly readings lands in those two unquantified bands.
So a reader at a hundred and twenty-three and a reader at sixty get the same label and the same advice.
That's the sentence. And for the record — one automated read of a government page gave us ranges for the upper two. We could not re-verify it anywhere, so we don't print it.
[warmly] Good.

Technology. Micron licensed Netlist's entire patent portfolio on the fifth of October. Thirty million US dollars a quarter for twenty quarters. Six hundred million in total, in the document's own words. Server memory modules and high-bandwidth memory. The trade commission terminated the parallel case against Samsung, Google and Super Micro on settlement. The evidentiary hearing had been set for the twenty-third of November.
[curious] So the patents that sit between your memory and your accelerator just got priced.
That's who collects the rent on the AI build-out.
You also found a threshold nobody will name.
Taiwan Semiconductor filed September revenue on Wednesday. A record quarter in Taiwan dollars. But it guides in US dollars, on an assumed rate of thirty-two.
So the beat depends on the currency.

Work backwards from its own figures and the top of guidance is reached only if the Taiwan dollar is stronger than thirty-two point six three. One wire converted at just under thirty-two and called it a beat. It's a miss. The company has published no dollar figure of its own.
[deadpan] Lovely.

The Kit is a lens. Sigma, fifty to one hundred and twenty millimetres, constant F two point eight, three hundred and ninety grams, seven hundred and ninety-nine US dollars. Everything measured about it was measured by its maker. The stabilisation figure is Sigma's own self-test on a body of Sigma's choosing. There is no independent bench result anywhere.
[skeptical] None?

None. And the reviewer who liked it still records that at fifty millimetres near minimum focus the corners get extremely soft and swirly — and that he was willing to overlook some pretty major image quality issues for the size and the price.
What did the forums say?
That's the finding. The post reproducing the press release had drawn exactly one reader comment. The companion live blog, none.
[laughs] A legend with one comment.
Twenty-four pre-order retailers listed across America and Europe. Not one of them in Asia.
The Atelier this week is reading lamps. And it opens with a document that doesn't exist any more.

The standard that put a number on flicker — I triple E seventeen eighty-nine — is marked inactive. Inactivation date, the twenty-sixth of March this year. Nothing. Its rule was usable: flicker not to exceed frequency times nought point nought eight. Ten per cent at a hundred and twenty hertz; four per cent if you're sensitive.
So what do the bulbs actually publish?
One maker's three sheets. The non-dimmable bulb measures under one per cent. The dimmable one, under six per cent at a hundred and twenty hertz — inside the general limit, outside the sensitive one.
[thoughtful] So the one behaviour you want at a bedside is the one nobody certifies.
And it's the cheap end that publishes. An eighteen-dollar bulb gives you the red value and the colour-shift figure. A nine-hundred-and-fifty-pound lamp publishes neither.
There's also a nice piece of plumbing in the sceptic box.
The design shop people use to compare lamps was acquired in April twenty twenty-one by the group that owns three of the houses it ranks.
[scoffs] So the comparison and the compared are one balance sheet.

And here it is a legal question too. A table lamp in Singapore is a controlled good. A circular in March fined a supplier fifteen thousand Singapore dollars for three unregistered items — and the ban applies regardless of whether the product is labelled for export only.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every single week.
Leathercraft. And it starts with one mechanical fact I did not know.

A sewing machine makes a lockstitch. One thread from above, one from below, knotted between the layers. Cut it anywhere and it unzips. Two needles on one thread, each passing through the same hole from opposite sides, so every stitch locks the one before. Cut it and it stops.
[excited] And no machine does it.

No machine does it. That single fact is why a craft with nearly a million people in its biggest forum still turns on a piece of toothed steel you hit with a mallet. The biggest subreddit runs eight hundred and eighty-eight thousand members — and grew three and a half per cent this year. Its beginner-facing sibling has sixty-eight thousand and grew nearly thirty-two.
So the old room is full and still.
The old guard lives on a forum with ninety-eight thousand members and three-quarters of a million posts since two thousand and six. And that forum is openly discussing its own decline.
[sighs] Go on.

A thread opened in February and still running in September. One moderator counted six hundred and two users online — and six logged in. Another supplied the diagnosis. YouTube also takes its share of folks who would rather just watch than participate.
[thoughtful] We have a lot of traffic, but most of it is window shopping.
That's the line of the week.
Now the argument. Because every hobby has one.

Pricking iron versus stitching chisel. The traditionalist says a pricking iron just does what it says — it makes a small prick marker to give equal spacing for the awl to follow. They will penetrate thin leather, especially if they are sharp. One marks. The other punches through and skips the awl entirely.
[amused] And whichever you own decides which tradition you joined, without anyone telling you.
French irons from the traditional house run from about sixty-five US dollars for two teeth to four hundred for fifteen. And on the day we looked, only ten of thirty-nine variants were in stock.
So availability is the tax, not price.
And here's the Singapore fact. One of the four maker names this hobby covets is based here.
[gasps] Here?

Crimson Hides. Its prices are in Singapore dollars, it says, where we are based. Its Japanese-style irons are one hundred and fifty-five Singapore dollars, with fourteen-tooth sizes in ready stock and about three weeks otherwise.
That is genuinely delightful. One of the top-shelf makers on earth ships from this island.

The sceptic box is about money, and it goes the other way to the story everyone tells. Hides got cheaper. The American producer-price index for hides and skins fell thirty-six per cent between January twenty twenty-three and December twenty twenty-five.
[skeptical] And the finished goods?

A Texas bootmaker, a hundred and eleven years old, said prices had risen by more than two hundred dollars a pair. And the largest hobby chain reported gross margin up five point three points — primarily due to better pricing of our products.
[scoffs] Better pricing of our products.
The raw material got cheaper and you did not.
And the tropical warning, because this is the bit that matters here.

Conservation guidance is explicit: leather needs a relative humidity under sixty-five per cent to keep. Singapore sits above sixty-five per cent most of the year. Vegetable-tanned leather lives in a dry box, not on a shelf. That's the whole Singapore chapter of this hobby in one sentence.
Culture, quickly, because the chart is lopsided.

Thursday's dailies are the only published numbers for this weekend. A nineteen-million-dollar horror film took three point six million on opening day. Aaron Sorkin's sequel took six hundred and fifty thousand in previews.
[laughs] Five to one, to the cheap one.
The critics went the other way. Eighteen per cent for the horror, fifty-six for the sequel.
And the fifty-six is a fall.

Yesterday we printed sixty-one from a hundred and twenty critics. Fifty-nine reviews later it's five points lower — which is what a score does when the early invited critics stop being the whole sample.
What's the argument in the comments?
Not whether it's good. Who made the first one. One reviewer: I've come to the conclusion that David Fincher actually deserves more credit.
[amused] Brutal.

The Good Life is a watch. A thirty-nine millimetre steel Voutilainen, estimated at a hundred and twenty to two hundred and forty thousand US dollars. One million and sixteen thousand with premium. Eight point four seven times the low estimate, and roughly eighteen per cent of the entire auction in one lot.
[gasps] One lot.
Forty-eight hours earlier the same market said no. A modern tourbillon at a fifty-to-seventy-thousand estimate did not sell at all.
So not independents are soaring.
Eight-piece provenance with an in-house movement is soaring. A modern limited edition cannot find a bid. Different markets wearing the same word.
Family Desk — and this is the four hundredths.
A harmonised meta-analysis of twelve thousand eight hundred and seventy-four young people, activity measured by accelerometer rather than asked about.
And twenty-six extra minutes a day buys?
Four hundredths of a standard deviation on the clustered risk score. Real, consistently signed, and small.
[deadpan] Four hundredths.

And two rows go the other way. The authors print them rather than bury them. More sitting was associated with slightly lower blood pressure. Weak, sensitive to the modelling approach, and heterogeneous across subgroups. Sitting time unlikely to be an important determinant. Singapore's own number, from a repeat survey of fifteen hundred parents. Weekly homework down to four point three hours from six point four six a decade ago. Up to two hundred and sixty dollars a month, from forty-eight, inflation-adjusted.
[exhales] The school gave the time back and the market took it.

Nearly ninety per cent agreed children spend too much time on tuition. Seven in ten said they'd spend more. Twenty people trained twelve weeks wearing the same running watch and were tested against a laboratory criterion before and after. It read about three millilitres per kilogram per minute high both times. It promised a finish seven and a half minutes faster than they actually ran.
[wry] So the watch is an optimist.

And travel, one line, because it's lovely. You can walk into the dome of an eight-point-two metre telescope at Paranal, every Saturday of the year, free. The one everyone pictures — the high array on the plateau — is shut, and was never open to the public anyway.
[warmly] Free, every Saturday. Put it in the calendar.

It's Saturday, so the Scoreboard. Thirty-four calls came due. Nineteen landed, thirteen missed, two cannot be settled. Micron, where we made the same call twice and graded it twice. One issue said revenue would clear fifty billion. Another said fifty, plus or minus one. Fifty-four point two three billion. The loose call won. The precise one missed by over three billion.
[laughs] So being specific lost.

Being specific lost to being right. That's the lesson and it is annoying. We put an Arctic agreement in November. It was signed on the twenty-second of September. The event happened; the month did not.
[chuckles] Half marks.
And the Long Read. India.
[thoughtful] This one changed my mind as I read it.

At Terminal Three of Delhi airport a driver named Mukesh Kumar explained how he's paid. For the first couple of months the platform gave him a hundred rupees a ride as a launch incentive. It stopped. And replaced the cash with free wheat flour, rice and lentils, redeemable at dairy-cooperative outlets.
[pause] A ride-hailing company paying its drivers in flour.

He'd prefer the cash. The company is Bharat Taxi, run by a multi-state cooperative registered last June and promoted by eight national cooperatives. The drivers are called Sarathis — from the Sanskrit for charioteer. The driver is the owner.
Now the numbers, because this is where I sat up.

From the minister's own written answer in August: eight hundred and forty-eight thousand registered drivers. Four and a half million registered customers. Eleven thousand one hundred and six. A day. Nationally.
[gasps] Eleven thousand. Against eight hundred and forty-eight thousand drivers.
That's about one and three tenths of one per cent. One ride, per registered driver, roughly every seventy-six days. Thirty thousand drivers. Three hundred and seventy-two rides a day.
[exhales] So it's failed.

That's the reasonable reading, and it's the wrong one. Look at what the thing actually delivers at scale. Eight hundred and forty-eight thousand self-employed people on a single register. Through which accident cover, a national health entitlement, group insurance and a bank's credit reach workers who own a vehicle, carry a loan and have no employer to reach them.
[drawn out] Ohhh.
The app isn't the product. The app is the enrolment mechanism. The welfare bundle is the product.
So as a business it's a catastrophe.
And as a census it's a triumph. India has built, more or less by accident, a union with an interface.
And a register that size is leverage even if nobody takes a ride.
The minister's own claim at the Gujarat launch is the admission — that the cooperative's arrival had already forced the private operators to revise their fares.
[thoughtful] So it sets prices without carrying passengers.
September in Ahmedabad was the first demonstration, and the ugliest. Drivers struck for four days, then began boycotting the private apps.
And there are allegations after that.

There are, and we hold them as allegations. An Indian technology title reported passengers surrounded and told to delete rival apps — and said plainly it could not verify the accounts, that sources feared going to the police, and that neither the platform nor either city's police chief responded.
Which is the honest way to carry it.
A platform that is winning does not need a cordon at an airport rank.
[pause] So what's the threshold here?

Nobody has set one, so we did. To be the app a driver opens first in one city, it needs something like a hundred thousand rides a day in that city alone. Nine times its present national volume. Eight hundred and forty-eight thousand registrations aren't traction. They're a mailing list.
And the question underneath it.
What happens when a government becomes the counterparty in a labour dispute it also arbitrates. India hasn't nationalised ride-hailing. It has nationalised the drivers' bargaining position.
[thoughtful] And it's discovering it can't control what they do with it.

That's the issue. Every desk this week had a line below which nothing happens, and somebody drew every one of them. A line drawn to describe will tell you its own range. A line drawn to be defended will not.
[warmly] Two of Singapore's four bands won't say where they begin.
Which is the most informative number in the issue.
[pause] Mm.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
